code_review_effort.title: Code review effort
code_review_effort.description: Effort tier for the delegated code review that performs each round: low, medium, high, xhigh or max. Those five are the only values the server accepts — anything else is refused at every review start, naming the value and this set, rather than reviewed at an unknown depth. Deeper tiers cost more money and wall-clock AND raise more comments, each of which a fix wave must resolve before the change request can flip ready.

code_review_model.title: Code review model
code_review_model.description: Model the delegated review runs on. The default is opus[1m]: the opus alias with the one-million-token context window, which is what lets a review load an epic-sized diff at all — the whole diff goes into the review's prompt before the model runs, so a bare alias meets a large change request with a prompt-too-long failure and no review. Whatever is set here is passed through verbatim, so naming a bare alias gives that window up. An alias — opus, sonnet, haiku — is the portable way to name a model, because it resolves against whatever provider the review's environment file points at; a pinned model id only means the same thing on the provider it came from. The [1m] suffix carries no such portability: it selects a long-context beta, and it was measured only on the first-party provider, where it is accepted on opus and sonnet and refused outright on haiku. On another provider — Bedrock, Vertex, a gateway — or on an account without that entitlement, it may be refused too, and a round that meets that is a failed round whose reason names this option; set it to a bare alias there. Leave empty to take that environment's own default instead.

code_review_claude_env_file.title: Code review environment file
code_review_claude_env_file.description: A file in .env format (KEY=value per line, # comments, optional quotes) whose variables are handed to the Claude agent that runs each review. This is how a review is given credentials, and it is required: the server forwards no authentication of its own, so without it a review reaches the reviewer as an anonymous caller and comes back having reviewed nothing. The variables are layered OVER the server's own environment, so the file need only carry what it changes. Read once, when the server starts — an edit takes effect in a new session.

observe_runs.title: Observe runs
observe_runs.description: Whether each /deliverer:refine or /deliverer:build run is observed, on by default. An observer is a separate process, started beside the run and never inside it: it reads the session records Claude Code already writes and produces a debrief — a short account of what the plugin's own machinery did and what it cost you, which you can forward to whoever maintains the plugin. It cannot slow, block, edit or fail a run: nothing it does reaches the run at all, and a run that fell over is observed exactly like one that finished. What it writes goes under the plugin's own data directory and never inside a repository, nothing is ever removed, and the debrief is bounded to the plugin — nothing from your repository, and no word of what you and the run said to each other. A line names the debrief when your run stops, and again on your next prompt if you did not see the first. Turn this off and nothing starts at all: no process, no trace and no debrief.
